title: How To Get Your Students To Like Your Class Rules https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2016/06/25/how-to-get-your-students-to-like-your-class-rules/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Building on an earlier article about explaining "why" behind classroom rules, Linsin adds a refinement: emphasize specifically how a student's non-compliance affects the people around them, not just the student personally. He argues this appeal to empathy is powerful for shifting attitudes and behavior, whereas failing to explain reasoning communicates antagonism and an authoritarian "my way or the highway" stance. Citing Adam Grant's book Originals, he notes that explaining rules' rationale not only increases compliance but helps children develop into more thoughtful, questioning future leaders. He also connects the practice to how misbehaving students respond emotionally afterward — when they understand a rule's purpose in advance, breaking it produces genuine remorse and reflection rather than mere compliance out of fear.
points: When explaining classroom rules, emphasize specifically how a student's non-compliance affects the people around them, not just themselves.
Explaining a rule's rationale doesn't mean it's negotiable — leadership and consistency are preserved while respect is communicated.
Citing Adam Grant's Originals, explaining "why" is linked to raising more thoughtful future leaders, not just better rule-followers.
Students who understand why a rule matters in advance feel genuine remorse when they break it, rather than just resentment at being caught.
quotes: Studies have shown that people are more likely to do what you ask if you give them a reason.
Just using the word “because” will make your rules more meaningful.
You see, the use of reasoning also sends the message that you respect your students. It sends the message that what is best for them is your highest priority.
To that end—and this is key here—be sure to include how their non-compliance of the rules affects those around them .
You communicate loud and clear that it’s your way or the highway , that they should do what you ask because you said so.

Interestingly, the research, as described in Adam Grant’s book Originals, shows that not only does explaining why lead to more rule following, it causes children to question rules that don’t line up with societal expectations.
Do this, and your students will eagerly jump on board your program.
